before.label: Social facts & collective life
before.description: Social facts, causes and functions, solidarity, ritual and collective thought provide distinct sociological questions. Hubert, Mauss, Simiand, Halbwachs and Meillet develop particular inquiries; historical and anthropological recipients adapt them selectively.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Émile Durkheim (1858–1917), The Division of Labour in Society (1893); influence on Bloch is substantial but selective and critical.

representative_people.context: Defines a sociological object, distinguishes causes from functions, and investigates conditions of solidarity and collective thought. His arguments and ethnographic assumptions require separate assessment.
representative_people.works: De la division du travail social (1893); Les Règles de la méthode sociologique (1895); Les Formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse (1912)

representative_people.context: Collaborative research on sacrifice and later work on gifts examine ritual relations and obligations; the two projects are not interchangeable.
representative_people.works: With Henri Hubert, “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899); “Essai sur le don” (1925)

representative_people.context: Coauthors a provisional comparative theory of sacrifice that distinguishes participants, consecration and mediation. His contribution is not absorbed into Mauss’s later gift essay.
representative_people.works: With Marcel Mauss, “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899)

representative_people.context: Pursues the methodological relation between historical evidence and social science. Annales explicitly reprints his intervention in 1960 as part of its continuing dialogue.
representative_people.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903; Annales reprint, 1960)

representative_people.context: Develops the social frameworks of remembering as a distinct inquiry. Later critical reuse and his intellectual formation are separate evidentiary questions.
representative_people.works: Les Cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); On Collective Memory (edited English collection, 1992)

representative_people.context: Explicitly applies Durkheim’s social-fact definition to language and investigates social conditions of semantic change.
representative_people.works: “Comment les mots changent de sens” (1906)

representative_people.context: A selective historical recipient and interlocutor, not a doctrinal adherent. His acknowledgment of Durkheim is documented in the scholarly introduction cited here.
representative_people.works: Feudal Society (1939–40); contextual reception study: Susan W. Friedman, Marc Bloch, Sociology and Geography

before.scope_note: Durkheim and selected collaborators, recipients and interlocutors, not a membership register. Collective explanation does not imply that all institutions are useful or all differentiation creates solidarity. Colonial-era categories and ethnographic generalizations remain claims to assess. Bloch’s engagement is selective; modernization and Bourdieu links still need more precise reception passages.

strands.title: Social facts and institutional resistance
strands.focus: Durkheim’s examples include obligations, signs and monetary practices. Externality and coercive capacity distinguish his object; mere statistical commonness does not suffice.
strands.works: Rules (1895), chapter I

strands.title: Origins, functions and critical antecedents
strands.focus: Chapter V disputes Comte’s and Spencer’s utility-based explanations: identifying a use does not explain an institution’s origin, and functions can change.
strands.works: Rules (1895), chapter V

strands.title: Differentiation and failures of solidarity
strands.focus: Division of labor can produce conflict and anomie. Durkheim’s discussion of crises and capital/labor antagonism qualifies any automatic equation of differentiation with cohesion.
strands.works: Division of Labour (1893), book III chapter I

strands.title: Religious life and collective categories
strands.focus: Sacred practices and collective membership are distinguished from a purely private belief. The proposed social formation of categories is an argument to assess, not an established origin of all thought.
strands.works: Elementary Forms (1912), introduction and religion definition

strands.title: Sacrifice, participants and mediation
strands.focus: Hubert and Mauss build on and revise earlier comparative scholarship. Their provisional model distinguishes ritual participants and movement between sacred and profane.
strands.works: “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899)

strands.title: Historical evidence and social science
strands.focus: Simiand’s methodological challenge and Bloch’s selective historical reception are different forms of engagement; Annales’ later reprint makes one continuing exchange explicit.
strands.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903; reprinted 1960); Bloch reception in Sociology and Geography

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering and language
strands.focus: Halbwachs’s memory inquiry and Meillet’s semantic history develop different objects from social relations. Shared vocabulary alone does not establish identical methods.
strands.works: Les Cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); “Comment les mots changent de sens” (1906)

before.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
before.date_label: Nineteenth-century roots; regional, cultural and ecological inquiry
before.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. Their later uses differ, including Annales geography and environmental historians’ landscape inquiry.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Paul Vidal de la Blache influences Febvre and Bloch; George Perkins Marsh, Man and Nature (1864), is an environmental precursor, not an Annales founder. Additional readings: Sauer, “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925); Leopold, A Sand County Almanac (1949).

representative_people.context: Investigates how human activity forms a region’s geographical individuality; engages Michelet’s national framing. His human geography is a resource for Annales, with the reception limits retained in the connection note.
representative_people.works: Tableau de la géographie de la France (1903)

representative_people.context: Studies human modification of physical environments; a precursor to environmental inquiry, not an Annales founder.
representative_people.works: Man and Nature; or, Physical Geography as Modified by Human Action (1864)

representative_people.context: Treats landscapes as related physical and cultural forms with histories; challenges rigid explanations from physical conditions alone.
representative_people.works: “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925)

representative_people.context: Conservationist whose ecological observation and teaching supplied one model for reading landscapes; Cronon later recalls workshops modeled on his course.
representative_people.works: A Sand County Almanac (1949)

representative_people.context: Uses local political boundaries and population distribution to examine ratification.
representative_people.works: The Geographical Distribution of the Vote (1894)

before.scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme.

outcomes.finding: Reviewed Bachelard’s preliminary discourse/chapter-one excerpt and Canguilhem’s own norm/average discussion and 1950 preface. Added explicit Halbwachs and Sorre resources, distinguishing Sorre’s post-draft confirmation. Prior Althusser/Foucault primary reception records remain valid and separate; retrospective intellectual maps are not converted wholesale into incoming arrows.
outcomes.research_limit: Canguilhem selected later-edition transcriptions, not full 1943/1955 originals. Original Halbwachs/Sorre, Bergson/Meyerson/Comte and Fontenelle texts remain unread; only explicit reception encoded. MIT English PDF404; full Foucault revision link via Elden failed; prior opening excerpt retained. UQAM omits bibliography, partly checked against complete-book transcription item53 and Sorre citations. Bachelard site’s erroneous1934heading rejected using independent1938metadata. The bounded question is resolved with these concrete access/edition limits, not a complete genealogy.
